subject: physics
title: Braking forces and large decelerations
key_idea: Brakes stop a vehicle by doing work against its motion, which removes kinetic energy and heats the brakes. A greater speed needs a greater braking force to stop in the same distance. Large decelerations are dangerous because of overheating, loss of control and large forces on people.

blocks.text: This section explains where the energy goes when a vehicle brakes.

items: The brakes apply a friction force between the brake and the wheel.
This friction force does work, which reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle.
The energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, so their temperature increases.
The greater the speed, the greater the braking force needed to stop in a certain distance.
The greater the braking force, the greater the deceleration.

blocks.label: Kinetic energy
where: kinetic energy is in joules, J
speed is in metres per second, m/s

blocks.label: Work done
where: work done is in joules, J

blocks.text: To stop a vehicle, the work done by the brakes must equal its initial kinetic energy.

items: Brakes do work, which removes kinetic energy and heats the brakes.
A greater braking force gives a greater deceleration.
A greater speed needs a greater braking force to stop in the same distance.

blocks.text: (Separate science) The work done by the brakes equals the initial kinetic energy. This shows how braking distance depends on speed.

items: Work done = braking force × braking distance.
Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × speed². It depends on the speed squared.
So for the same braking force, braking distance depends on speed squared.
Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times greater, so the braking distance is four times greater.

blocks.label: Braking distance
where: braking distance is in metres, m
speed is the initial speed, in metres per second, m/s
deceleration is in metres per second squared, m/s²

Doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times greater.
The work done by the brakes equals the initial kinetic energy.

blocks.text: A large deceleration needs a large braking force, in a short time or distance. This causes three dangers.

items: The brakes can overheat, because more work is done and more energy is transferred to them.
The driver can lose control of the vehicle.
A large force acts on the people in the vehicle, which can cause injury.

blocks.label: Force
where: acceleration is in metres per second squared, m/s²

blocks.text: A deceleration is a negative acceleration. A bigger deceleration means a bigger force on the car and on the people inside it.
Estimating the force on a car

items: Typical car speeds are about 13 m/s in a town and about 30 m/s on a motorway.
Typical emergency decelerations are a few m/s², up to about 6 m/s².

items.text: A typical car has a mass of about 1500 kg.
In an emergency stop a car might decelerate at about 6 m/s².

worked_example.question:
Two identical cars were driven along a straight, level road. One car had a greater speed than the other car. The driver of each car applied the brakes until the cars stopped. Both cars travelled the same distance while braking.

Explain how braking from a greater speed affected the risk of the brakes overheating.
answer_points: The faster car has more kinetic energy (or the frictional / braking force is greater).
So more work is done by the brakes to stop the faster car (more energy is transferred).
So the risk of the brakes overheating is greater for the faster car.
worked_example.tip: The third mark depends on one of the first two. More heating on its own is ignored.

worked_example.question:
Car B brakes and comes to a stop.

Estimate the force acting on car B when it decelerates at 6 m / s².
Use the equation: force = mass × acceleration
For the mass in the equation, use an estimate of the mass of car B.
answer_points: Estimate the mass of the car as 1500 kg.
worked_example.tip: Any answer from 2400 N to 21 000 N scores 3 marks. A mass estimate from 400 kg to 3500 kg is allowed.
